The next morning, people almost followed Abbé Pirard through the streets, and shopkeepers came to the doors of their shops when he went to petition the judges on the marquis’s behalf. For the first time, he was received politely by them. The stern Jansenist, indignant at everything he saw, worked at length with the lawyers he had chosen for the Marquis de La Mole and left for Paris. He was weak enough to tell two or three friends from the seminary, who accompanied him as far as the carriage whose coat of arms they admired, that after administering the seminary for fifteen years, he was leaving Besançon with five hundred and twenty francs in savings. These friends embraced him in tears, and said among themselves:

“The good abbé could have spared himself that lie; it really is far too ridiculous.”

The common people, blinded by the love of money, were incapable of understanding that it was in his sincerity that Abbé Pirard had found the strength necessary to struggle alone for six years against Marie Alacoque, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Jesuits, and his bishop.




CHAPTER XXX

AN AMBITIOUS MAN

    There is now only one true rank of nobility, and that is the title of duke;
    marquis is ridiculous; at the word duke, heads turn.

    EDINBURGH REVIEW.


The abbé was astonished by the marquis’s noble bearing and almost cheerful tone. Yet this future minister received him without any of those little grand-seigneur airs, so polite, but so impertinent to anyone who understands them. That would have been time wasted, and the marquis was sufficiently involved in great affairs to have no time to waste.

For six months, he had been intriguing to have a certain ministry accepted simultaneously by the king and the nation, a ministry that, out of gratitude, would make him a duke.

For many years, the marquis had vainly asked his lawyer in Besançon for a clear and precise report on his lawsuits in Franche-Comté. How could the celebrated lawyer have explained them to him when he did not understand them himself?

The little square sheet of paper the abbé handed him explained everything.

“My dear abbé,” the marquis said to him, after disposing in less than five minutes of all the formulas of politeness and inquiries about personal matters, “my dear abbé, amid my supposed prosperity, I lack the time to attend seriously to two small matters that are nevertheless fairly important: my family and my affairs. I look after the fortune of my house on a grand scale; I can carry it far. I look after my pleasures, and that is what must come before everything else, at least in my eyes,” he added, catching the astonishment in Abbé Pirard’s eyes.

Though a sensible man, the abbé was amazed to see an old man speak so frankly of his pleasures.

“Work undoubtedly exists in Paris,” the great lord continued, “but perched on the fifth floor; and as soon as I draw closer to a man, he takes an apartment on the second floor, and his wife establishes a reception day; consequently, there is no more work, no more effort except to be, or to appear to be, a man of the world. That is their sole concern as soon as they have bread to eat.

“For my lawsuits, strictly speaking, and even for each lawsuit considered separately, I have lawyers who work themselves to death; one of them died of consumption the day before yesterday. But for my affairs in general, would you believe, monsieur, that for three years I have given up trying to find a man who, while writing for me, deigns to think a little seriously about what he is doing? Besides, all this is merely a preface.

“I esteem you, and I would venture to add, although I am seeing you for the first time, I love you. Will you be my secretary, at a salary of eight thousand francs, or even twice that? I shall still gain by it, I swear to you; and I shall make it my business to preserve your fine parish for you, for the day when we no longer suit one another.”

The abbé refused, but toward the end of the conversation, the genuine predicament in which he saw the marquis suggested an idea to him.

“I left behind, in the depths of my seminary,” he told the marquis, “a poor young man who, unless I am mistaken, is going to be harshly persecuted there. If he were merely a simple religious, he would already be in pace.

“So far, this young man knows only Latin and Holy Scripture; but it is not impossible that one day he may display great talents either for preaching or for the direction of souls. I do not know what he will do, but he has the sacred fire; he may go far. I had intended to give him to our bishop, if ever we had been sent one who shared something of your way of judging men and affairs.”

“Where does your young man come from?” said the marquis.

“He is said to be the son of a carpenter from our mountains, but I would sooner believe him the natural son of some rich man. I saw him receive an anonymous or pseudonymous letter with a bill of exchange for five hundred francs.”

“Ah! That is Julien Sorel,” said the marquis.

“How do you know his name?” said the astonished abbé; and when he blushed at his own question:

“That is something I shall not tell you,” replied the marquis.

“Well then,” the abbé resumed, “you might try making him your secretary; he has energy and judgment; in short, it is an experiment worth trying.”

“Why not?” said the marquis. “But would he be the sort of man to let the prefect of police or anyone else grease his palm to act as a spy in my house? That is my only objection.”

After Abbé Pirard’s favorable assurances, the marquis took out a thousand-franc note:

“Send this traveling money to Julien Sorel; have him come to me.”

“The habit of living in Paris must indeed, Monsieur le Marquis, produce this illusion in your mind; because you occupy a high social position, you do not know the tyranny that weighs upon us poor provincials, and particularly upon priests who are not friends of the Jesuits. They will not be willing to let Julien Sorel leave; they will know how to cloak themselves in the cleverest pretexts. I shall be told that he is ill, the post will have lost the letters, and so on and so forth.”

“One of these days I shall obtain a letter from the minister to the bishop,” said the marquis.

“I was forgetting a precaution,” said the abbé. “Although this young man was born very low, he has a proud spirit; he will be of no use whatsoever in your affairs if his pride is alarmed; you would make him stupid.”

“I like that,” said the marquis. “I shall make him my son’s companion; will that suffice?”

Some time later, Julien received a letter in an unfamiliar hand and bearing the Châlon postmark. In it he found a payment order upon a merchant in Besançon and instructions to go to Paris without delay. The letter was signed with an assumed name, but upon opening it Julien had started: a large blot of ink had fallen in the middle of the thirteenth word. It was the signal he had agreed upon with Abbé Pirard.
